questions.q: What Setup object is the foundation for OAuth-based authentication of an inbound integration?
options: An External Credential
A Named Credential
A Connected App
A Permission Set Group
questions.explain: A Connected App defines the OAuth scopes, callback URL, and certificate used to authenticate an external application calling into Salesforce.

questions.q: What distinguishes the OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer Flow from the Client Credentials Flow?
options: JWT Bearer is only usable for SOAP callouts; Client Credentials only for REST
There is no real difference between the two flows
JWT Bearer requires an interactive browser login; Client Credentials does not
JWT Bearer uses a certificate-based signed token with no client secret transmitted per request; Client Credentials authenticates with a client ID and secret
questions.explain: JWT Bearer relies on a signed JSON Web Token verified against an uploaded certificate, avoiding transmitting a secret at request time, while Client Credentials exchanges a client ID and secret.

questions.q: Why is granting a System Administrator profile to an integration user considered a serious security mistake?
options: Because it violates least privilege — any compromise of that one credential would compromise the entire org, instead of being limited to what the integration actually needs
Because System Administrator profiles are incompatible with Connected Apps
Because it prevents the integration from authenticating at all
Because System Administrator profiles cannot use OAuth
questions.explain: An integration user should get only the specific object/field permissions the integration needs; an overly broad profile multiplies the damage if that one credential is ever compromised.

questions.q: What is the relationship between authentication and authorization for an inbound call?
options: They are the same thing — once authenticated, a caller can do anything
Authentication confirms who is calling; authorization (via the underlying user's profile/permission sets) separately determines what that caller is actually allowed to read or write
Authorization happens before authentication in every Salesforce flow
Authorization only applies to SOAP web services, not REST
questions.explain: A successfully authenticated caller still runs as some Salesforce user, and that user's permissions are a separate, independent check on what the call can actually do.

questions.q: What additional layer of control can an admin apply beyond OAuth for a server-to-server integration calling from a fixed, known set of servers?
options: Switching the integration to SOAP, which has no authentication requirement
Disabling API access entirely
Restricting the integration user's profile with Trusted IP Ranges or Login IP Ranges
Removing the Connected App's certificate
questions.explain: IP restrictions add a second layer of defense beyond OAuth itself, limiting where valid credentials can actually be used from.
